description: Ivorian reggae star Alpha Blondy opens his 1987 album Revolution with this dreamy love song, remembering Fanta Diallo walking on rainbows and kissing him on burning rocks — before the memory turns bittersweet.

pops.text: Alpha Blondy was born Seydou Koné on January 1, 1953, in Dimbokro, Ivory Coast. He grew up to become one of the world's most popular reggae artists.
This is the opening track of Revolution, released in 1987 and credited to Alpha Blondy and the Solar System, his big backing band.
Revolution found Blondy trying a mellower sound. On this track he adapted violins and cello to his usual reggae beat — strings and skanking, together at last.
Blondy sings in many tongues across his career, including Dioula, French, English, Hebrew and Arabic. This one is sung mostly in English.
The lyric is pure memory: 'Fanta walking on the rainbow, Fanta kissing me on the burning rocks.' Then, one day, Fanta flees away — and he keeps asking where she's gone.
The song takes a darker turn near the end: the last time he saw Fanta was at a psychiatric hospital, and he admits, 'Now I know that I did you wrong.'
Before the fame, Blondy studied English in New York at Hunter College and in Columbia University's American Language Program, playing open mikes on the side.
He is often called the Bob Marley of Africa. He even recorded the title track of Cocody Rock in Jamaica with Marley's own backing group, the Wailers.
Blondy later returned to Kingston's Tuff Gong Studios to record his 1986 album Jerusalem, again backed by the Wailers.
Decades on, the song still travels: Blondy performed it at Live 8 in Paris in 2005, and it remains one of his best-known songs.

title: Sweet Fanta Diallo

description: Dewey Bunnell's sun-warmed 1972 hit for America turns a childhood flat tire, some lizard-shaped clouds and a road sign for Ventura into soft rock's defining open-road daydream.

pops.text: Written and sung by Dewey Bunnell, this was the lead single from America's second album, Homecoming, released in 1972.
It reached No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 43 in the UK — America's third straight Top 10 hit back home.
Those 'alligator lizards in the air' were cloud shapes Bunnell saw in 1963, aged 11, while his father changed a flat tire near Vandenberg Air Force Base in California.
Standing by the road that day, the Bunnell boys also spotted a sign for Ventura. The town's name stuck around for nine years until it became a chorus.
There is no actual Ventura Highway. Bunnell meant the Pacific Coast Highway, Highway 1, which runs up to the town of Ventura.
The opening line about chewing on a piece of grass came from Bunnell's boyhood in Omaha, Nebraska, walking through cornfields.
The song is a 'go west' conversation between a hopeful kid and an old man named Joe, modeled on a grumpy old-timer Bunnell met in Biloxi, Mississippi.
Listen for the words 'purple rain' in the lyric — a full 12 years before Prince made the phrase famous in 1984.

About that George Martin credit: America produced the original themselves. Martin, the Beatles' producer, later remixed the track for their 1975 greatest-hits album History, and produced seven America albums in all.
The opening guitar riff got a second life in 2001, sampled all through Janet Jackson's hit 'Someone to Call My Lover.' Bunnell said the sample boosted America's sales.

title: Ventura Highway

description: A supergroup in disguise: Police drummer Stewart Copeland and jazz bass giant Stanley Clarke back singer-songwriter Deborah Holland on this working-day weary, sundown-hopeful gem from Animal Logic's 1989 debut.

pops.text: Animal Logic was a trio with a serious rhythm section: Stewart Copeland of the Police on drums and jazz fusion legend Stanley Clarke on bass.
The singer out front is Deborah Holland, who wrote or co-wrote every song the band recorded. Copeland and Clarke found her after wading through hundreds of demo tapes and auditions.
The band first came together in 1987, when Copeland and Clarke were booked to play a series of dates together in Brazil and decided to build a group.
Holland co-wrote this track with Frankie Blue. Its story is a working day: low wages, a hard boss, and one promise to hold onto.
That promise is the refrain: as soon as the sun goes down, she'll be with the one she loves — 'I'll be alright.' It is also where this streaming title comes from.
On the band's 1989 debut album the song appeared under its full title, 'As Soon as the Sun Goes Down.' The 2020 streaming reissue titled #1' lists it by its refrain: 'I'll Be Alright.'
It was released as a single from the debut and picked up airplay across pop, rock and adult-contemporary radio in the US.
The band recorded for I.R.S. Records, the label run by Miles Copeland — Stewart's brother, and the Police's manager.
Even the debut album cover has a Police connection: it was originally conceived for a Police greatest-hits album.

The trio toured the world in 1989 and appeared on Letterman and The Tonight Show, then split after 1991's Animal Logic II — before reuniting in 2022 with two new songs, 'Can You Tell Me' and 'Ordinary.'

title: I'll Be Alright

description: Otis Redding wrote it, but Aretha Franklin rebuilt it on Valentine's Day 1967 — flipping its perspective, spelling out the title, and turning a plea into a demand that became her signature song.

pops.text: Otis Redding wrote 'Respect' and released his version in 1965; it reached No. 35 on the pop chart. After hearing Aretha's, Redding joked, 'That girl took it away from me.'
Aretha had been performing the song live for about two years before she ever recorded it. She arrived at the studio with her arrangement already worked out.
She recorded it on Valentine's Day, February 14, 1967, at Atlantic's New York studio. Engineer Tom Dowd had also engineered Redding's original version.
Working with her sisters Carolyn and Erma at a piano in a small Detroit apartment, Aretha flipped the song from a man's plea into a woman's demand.
The famous spelled-out bridge — 'R-E-S-P-E-C-T, find out what it means to me' — was the Franklin sisters' addition. Redding's version had nothing like it.
Carolyn also suggested 'take care, TCB' — TCB being slang for 'taking care of business.' Aretha jumped on it, and the 'sock it to me' line was born in the same sessions.
The saxophone break is King Curtis, playing over chord changes borrowed from Sam & Dave's 'When Something Is Wrong With My Baby.'
The Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section played on the record in New York, after the album's Alabama sessions broke down. Aretha herself plays the driving piano part.
Released in April 1967, 'Respect' spent two weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and eight weeks atop the R&B chart, and won Aretha her first two Grammy Awards.
In 2021 Rolling Stone placed 'Respect' at No. 1 on its list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time. The Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry in 2002.

title: Respect

description: Atlanta collective Arrested Development put a homeless man's dignity on Top 40 radio in 1992: Speech's story of Mr. Wendal, who trades knowledge for a pair of shoes, peaked at No. 6 — and half its royalties went to help the homeless.

pops.text: This was the third single from Arrested Development's debut album, 3 Years, 5 Months and 2 Days in the Life Of..., released as a single on December 7, 1992.
Frontman Speech — born Todd Thomas — wrote and produced the track. The songwriting credits also name Sylvester Stewart, better known as Sly Stone.
Mr. Wendal is a fictional homeless man. Speech raps that he never thought twice about 'an ol' bum' until he got to know one — and learned from him.
In the song's exchange, Speech gives Mr. Wendal money and buys him shoes; Mr. Wendal gives back knowledge. 'It's not charity,' goes the idea — it's a trade between equals.
The group put its money where its message was: half of the single's royalties were donated to the National Coalition for the Homeless.
The song peaked at No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100, sold 500,000 copies and earned a gold certification — a Top 10 hit about homelessness.
In Europe and Australia it was issued as a double A-side with the group's next single, 'Revolution.'
The music video was directed by Keith Ward, and it received a nomination at the 1994 Soul Train Music Awards.
Arrested Development formed in Atlanta in 1988, founded by Speech and DJ Headliner as a positive, Afrocentric alternative to the gangsta rap of the day.

The debut album's title is literal — the time between the group's formation and signing its first record deal. It sold over four million copies in the US, and in 1993 the group became the first rap act to win the Grammy for Best New Artist.

title: Mr. Wendal

description: The debut single from prog supergroup Asia, written in an afternoon by John Wetton and Geoff Downes. It took a band of 1970s prog royalty to No. 4 in America and became their signature song.

pops.text: A supergroup in full: John Wetton from King Crimson, Steve Howe from Yes, Geoff Downes from the Buggles and Yes, and Carl Palmer from Emerson, Lake & Palmer.
This was the last song written and recorded for the debut album. Geffen's John Kalodner asked for a single, and Wetton and Downes wrote it in an afternoon.
Wetton had the chorus, Downes had the verse. Wetton said the chorus began life as a 6/8 country song before they moved the time signatures around.
The lyrics are, in Wetton's words, an abject apology for his dreadful behaviour toward a particular woman — one he later married, and divorced 10 years later.
Steve Howe overdubbed his Gibson Les Paul Junior playing the verse power chords seven times, each through a different amplifier, chasing a grungy sound.
In the middle eight, Howe doubled Downes' synth lick on a koto. Prog habits die hard, even on a three-and-a-half-minute pop single.
That line about catching a pearl and riding a dragon's wings? Wetton took it from Roger Dean's artwork for the album cover.
It peaked at No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 and spent six non-consecutive weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart in 1982.
The album spent nine weeks at No. 1 in the US and was Billboard's top album of 1982 — yet back home in Britain, this single only reached No. 46.
Afterlife: Cartman sang it to Congress in South Park's 'Kenny Dies,' Sam woke up to it on a loop in Supernatural's 'Mystery Spot,' and it turned up in The 40-Year-Old Virgin.

title: Heat Of The Moment

description: Leadoff track from The Honest Hour (2004), Assembly of Dust's first live album, recorded in Troy, New York. Reid Genauer's autobiographical opener about marriage, Cornell business school and starting over after Strangefolk.

pops.text: First song, first statement: this is the leadoff track on The Honest Hour, Assembly of Dust's first live album. The plan starts on track one.

It's loosely autobiographical: Reid Genauer's artist bio says the song documents his first year after Strangefolk — getting married, enrolling in business school at Cornell, and forming Assembly of Dust.
Yes, it's live: The Honest Hour was culled from a show in Troy, New York in early 2004, and the Daily Vault review specifies the venue — Revolution Hall in Troy.
Live, but polished: the band cleaned up audience noise on the recording, so the set plays with studio-like clarity while keeping its live energy and spontaneity.
Album facts: The Honest Hour was released September 14, 2004 on Hybrid Recordings, with nine songs mixing new Assembly of Dust material and reimagined versions of songs Genauer wrote for Strangefolk.
Hear the Steely Dan in it: a Home Grown Music Network review describes this opener's piano-driven beat in the Fagen-and-Becker mold, with words and melody winding together through Manhattan gridlock.

The backstory runs deep: Genauer co-founded Vermont band Strangefolk about a decade earlier while studying environmental science at the University of Vermont, then left and formed Assembly of Dust in 2002.
The plan included a degree: Genauer completed an MBA at Cornell, then balanced touring with a day job as Director of Creative Marketing at eMusic.com, according to his artist bio.
Writing team: Genauer and keyboardist Nate Wilson were the band's core writers, in a quintet rounded out by Adam Terrell on lead guitar, John Leccese on bass and Andy Herrick on drums.

File under 'hick funk': that was the label applied to Assembly of Dust's sound, which drew comparisons to Paul Simon, CSNY and The Band, with influences including Steely Dan, J.J. Cale and Little Feat.

title: Man with a Plan

description: A mostly instrumental funk workout from a band of Scotsmen that topped the US chart in 1975. Its only lyric is the title, shouted like a pep talk the broke band was giving itself.

pops.text: Yes, they were Scottish. Average White Band formed in London in 1972, playing American funk and R&B — and out-funking almost everybody at it.
The band's name was a joke from a friend in the diplomatic service, who used to remark that places were 'too hot for the average white man.'
It started with a guitar line from Hamish Stuart. Saxophonist Roger Ball then wrote the first part of that nagging horn melody.
This is essentially an instrumental. The only words in the whole song are the title, shouted at intervals like a chant.
Producer Arif Mardin, Atlantic's soul maestro, tightened the arrangement, beefed up the horns and highlighted the chant when the band re-recorded much of the album in New York.
Saxophonist Malcolm 'Molly' Duncan argued against releasing it as a single: it was, he said, a funk instrumental played by Scotsmen with no lyrics other than a shout.
Duncan said the shout was about picking yourself up when things aren't going well — relevant, because the band had spent a long time making no money whatsoever.
Released in Britain in July 1974, it failed to chart. American radio picked it up instead, and on 22 February 1975 it topped the Billboard Hot 100 for a week.
The J.B.'s reportedly answered it with 'Pick Up the Pieces One by One,' released under the name A.A.B.B. — Above Average Black Band. Touché.
After its American success it finally charted at home, reaching No. 6 in the UK. The single went gold in the US, and the album AWB hit No. 1 there too.

title: Pick Up the Pieces

description: The opening track of Harvest, the fourth album by Colombian psychedelic funk trio BALTHVS, recorded during a month in a tropical house in La Mesa. Sun-drenched, slow and quietly groovy.

pops.text: BALTHVS are a psychedelic funk trio from Bogotá, Colombia: Balthazar Aguirre on guitar, Johanna Mercuriana on bass and Santiago Lizcano on drums — all three sing.
Pronunciation guide: a live review renders the name 'bôl + thus.' The V is doing the job of a U, Roman-style.
The band formed in 2020. By the time Harvest arrived in 2024, they had already released three albums — this was their fourth.
All three members are credited as composers here. Harvest was the first BALTHVS album composed by all three of them together.
The album was recorded over a month at a tropical summer house in La Mesa, Colombia. The band brought their own gear, wanting nature over a sterile studio.
It was so hot in La Mesa that the only air conditioning was in the recording room — and that was to protect the equipment from overheating, not the band.
Shazam's metadata clocks this one at 91 BPM. This is a groove built for swaying, not sprinting.
The trio's recipe: Middle Eastern melody, disco, house, funk, psychedelia, surf and Colombian cumbia, all in the same pot.
Bookend trick: this opens Harvest, and the album closes with 'Sun Colored Eyes, Pt. 1' and 'Sun Colored Eyes, Pt. 2' — the same sunrise, twice more.
In November 2024, Berkeley act Bay Ledges remixed this song in a sample-driven bedroom-pop style — and NPR had already used a soundbite of it under a story about a Montana heat wave.

title: Sun Colored Eyes

description: Bananarama turned a London heatwave — and being stuck at work while everyone else holidayed — into a synth-pop classic. A year later, The Karate Kid carried it into America's Top 10.

pops.text: Released on 27 June 1983 as a stand-alone single. It was later folded into the group's second, self-titled album in 1984.
This was the first Bananarama hit the trio actually co-wrote. Sara Dallin, Siobhan Fahey and Keren Woodward wrote the lyrics with producers Steve Jolley and Tony Swain.
The inspiration was a rare London heatwave: the three were stuck in the city working while their friends were off enjoying holidays. Summer, but make it resentful.
Jolley and Swain built the backing track first, mixing steel drums with gritty guitar. Dallin has said the song is about the darker side of summer.
It reached No. 8 in the UK in 1983 and got the group onto Top of the Pops that July. Its biggest chart peak anywhere was No. 1 in Luxembourg.
The video was shot in New York in the summer of 1983 — Fahey admitted it was partly an excuse to get the group to New York for the first time.
The clip riffs on The Dukes of Hazzard: a bumbling cop duo chases the trio as they escape in a truck — at one point Bananarama throw bananas at the police cruiser.
In 1984 the song soundtracked Daniel's rough patches in The Karate Kid. Bananarama refused to put it on the film's soundtrack album — and it still became their first US Top 10 hit, at No. 9.
They revisited it in 1989 as 'Cruel Summer '89,' a new jack swing remix that reached No. 19 in the UK. The remix video was a compilation — the group was away on a world tour.
In 1998 Ace of Base covered it at their labels' request: their version hit No. 10 in the US, went gold, and matched the original's No. 8 peak in the UK.

title: Cruel Summer

description: Barbara Lewis wrote this dreamy soul classic herself and recorded it at Chicago's Chess Studios in January 1963. It topped the R&B chart and reached No. 3 pop.

pops.text: Barbara Lewis wrote this one herself — rare for a young singer in 1963, when most artists were handed songs to record.
The title came from gigs she played with her musician father in Detroit, where people would greet him: 'Hey stranger, hello stranger, it's been a long time!'
Listen closely: after the opening line, the words 'hello stranger' never appear again in the whole song.
It was recorded in January 1963 at Chess Studios in Chicago — hallowed ground for Muddy Waters and Chuck Berry.
That signature swirling organ riff is keyboardist John Young, on an arrangement by Riley Hampton, who was then working with Etta James.
The 'shoo-bop, shoo-bop, my baby' backing vocals are The Dells — producer Ollie McLaughlin recruited the whole group for the session.
Thirteen takes to nail it. On playback, Dell Chuck Barksdale reportedly kept jumping up and down shouting, 'It's a hit, it's a hit!'
He was right: the single spent two weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's R&B chart and crossed over to No. 3 on the Hot 100.
Atlantic nearly sat on it, fearing it sounded too much like Ruby & the Romantics' 'Our Day Will Come' — that hit's success got it released.
Yvonne Elliman took it back up the charts in 1977 — No. 15 pop and four weeks at No. 1 on the Easy Listening chart. Queen Latifah covered it in 2004, too.

title: Hello Stranger

description: North Carolina jamgrass outfit Barefoot Manner stretch out on the J.J. Cale standard made famous by Eric Clapton, turning it into a nearly nine-minute groove on Miles of Texas (2011).

pops.text: Yes, THAT 'After Midnight' — written by Tulsa songwriter J.J. Cale, who first released it as a single back in 1966.
Cale's original barely made a ripple. It took Eric Clapton's cover to turn it into a standard every jam band knows.
Delaney Bramlett introduced Clapton to Cale's music. Clapton cut it for his self-titled solo debut album in 1970.
Cale had no idea Clapton had recorded his song until he heard it on his car radio — he was, in his words, dirt poor and playing bar gigs at the time.
Clapton played it fast. Cale's own 1972 re-recording on Naturally slowed it way back down — Barefoot Manner split the difference and jam it out.
Barefoot Manner formed in North Carolina in winter 2000 as an acoustic trio, then grew into a quintet by 2003.
The lineup behind the band's sound: Hank Smith on banjo, Shawn Chase on mandolin, Jeff Garland on drums and washboard.
Clapton's version peaked at No. 18 on the Hot 100 in 1970 and became one of his signature songs — he even re-recorded it for a 1987 Michelob commercial.
This cut runs almost nine minutes — classic Barefoot Manner, a band fans and fellow musicians alike say is best heard live.
The band was enough of a live institution to inspire its own festivals: Camp Barefoot in Virginia and their own Mannerland gathering.

title: After Midnight

description: From Born on a Pirate Ship (1996), this wistful break-in ballad — co-written by Steven Page and Ed Robertson — became Barenaked Ladies' first US Billboard Hot 100 entry.

pops.text: Steven Page has said this was partly inspired by The Smiths' 'Back to the Old House' — another song about returning to a former home.
Misreading alert: Ed Robertson insists the narrator is NOT stalking an ex. The couple is still together — they just bought a house on Toronto's Danforth.
Yes, that's a musical saw in the personnel credits — Gene Hardy plays it, alongside Page and Robertson's guitars.
The song first appeared on 1996's Born on a Pirate Ship, recorded while the band was a quartet — Kevin Hearn hadn't joined yet.
Hearn still shows up in this video, even though he didn't play a note on the studio recording.
The video was directed by fellow Canadian Jason Priestley — Brandon Walsh himself — who suggested it because he was a fan.
Priestley also brought the band onto Beverly Hills, 90210 to perform at the Peach Pit After Dark — a big early US break.
The video earned a Best Director nomination at the 1997 MuchMusic Video Awards.
Chart history: No. 14 in Canada, and the band's very first entry on the US Billboard Hot 100, where it peaked at No. 88.
Tech time capsule: Apple included this music video on the Mac OS 8 installation CD as a QuickTime demo.

title: The Old Apartment

description: The live Rock Spectacle (1996) recording of Steven Page's tribute to the Beach Boys' Brian Wilson — the version US radio fell for, produced by Michael Phillip Wojewoda.

pops.text: Steven Page wrote this in his parents' basement around his 20th birthday, in 1990 — a love letter to Beach Boys genius Brian Wilson.
The opening scene is real: Page's late-night trips downtown to Sam the Record Man on Toronto's Yonge Street to check out the record shop.
The darker verses mirror Wilson's years under controversial psychologist Eugene Landy, who took over much of Wilson's life and career.
This song has at least five official recordings — Page himself said it's the most-recorded song in the band's catalogue.
Versions include a never-released 1990 cassette, the 1991 Yellow Tape, 1992's Gordon album — and this 1996 live take from Rock Spectacle.
But this live Rock Spectacle version is the one that broke in the US, reaching No. 68 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 23 on Alternative Airplay.
The label hedged with a shorter studio remake, 'Brian Wilson 2000,' fearing radio wouldn't play a long live track. Radio played the live one anyway.
Rock Spectacle producer Michael Phillip Wojewoda shares the artist billing on this recording — he also produced the original Gordon album.
The ultimate tribute: Brian Wilson covered this song himself, on his Live at the Roxy Theatre album in 2000.
Wilson later played his version for the band in person and asked, 'Is it cool?' His parting advice to them: 'Don't eat too much.'

title: Brian Wilson

description: The lead single from Paul's Boutique (1989), built by the Dust Brothers from a dense collage of disco and funk samples, cowbell included. It hit No. 36 on the Hot 100.

pops.text: This was the lead single from Paul's Boutique, released July 25, 1989 — the same day as the album.
Producers the Dust Brothers built these tracks as dense club instrumentals. They were surprised the Beasties wanted to rhyme over something so busy.
At least 15 samples are packed into this one song — the full album stitches together more than 100.
Dig in and you'll hear Sweet's 'The Ballroom Blitz' — that wobbly 'she thinks she's the passionate one' line is lifted straight from it.
Also in the mix: Kool & the Gang's 'Jungle Boogie,' Deep Purple's 'Hush,' the Commodores' 'Machine Gun' and James Brown's 'Funky President.'
And yes — the famous cowbell solo. A disembodied hand drops from the ceiling to play it in the video.
The video, directed by Adam Bernstein, is a full Saturday Night Fever and Dolemite homage — polyester, platform shoes and disco balls.
Chart first: this was the first single ever to crack the Top 20 of BOTH the Hot Rap Singles (No. 10) and Modern Rock Tracks (No. 18) charts.
On the Hot 100 it peaked at No. 36 — and it was the only charting single from Paul's Boutique.
Paul's Boutique was a commercial disappointment on release, then got canonized — now routinely ranked among the greatest hip-hop albums ever made.

title: Hey Ladies
